title: Blessings for everything
hookLine: Scottish Highland blessings, collected as Carmina Gadelica, for kindling fire, milking, sleep

lines: A BLESSING WHILE THE FIRE CATCHES.
cards: Morning in a Highland cottage. Last night the fire was banked low, the embers covered over to keep them alive. Now someone kneels at the hearth with cold hands, uncovers the glow, adds fuel, and blows it back into flame.
And while doing it, they say a blessing. Not in church: at the hearth, with the version coming under the door.
A collector named Alexander Carmichael went around the Highlands and islands of Scotland writing down prayers like that, and published them as Carmina Gadelica. Today: blessings for everything.

teach.b: Carmina Gadelica is Latin for Gaelic songs.

Inside are blessings for the jobs of an ordinary day: kindling the fire in the morning, banking it again at night, milking the cow, churning, weaving cloth, setting out on a journey, lying down to sleep.

Carmichael heard them from working people and printed the Gaelic beside his English, polishing some as he went. Nothing is too small. The fire blessing doesn't wait for a holy moment; lighting the fire is the holy moment.
The first letter to Timothy says it: "every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving: For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer."
Brother Lawrence turned his cake for the love of God. These blessings go a step further and give each chore its own words.
Paul writes to the Colossians: "whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus." Whatsoever. The Gaelic blessings take it at face value.
Christ, Mary, the saints and the angels are invited into the cowshed, the kitchen and the boat. The fire at night is banked in God's name, so the house is kept while everyone sleeps.
The milking blessing turns a cold dawn chore into a moment of company.

teach.h: A BLESSING TIES ATTENTION TO THE JOB.
teach.b: A blessing also ties attention to the job; it's hard to scroll a phone and bless the milking at once. And something tender: work nobody thanks you for, done in front of someone who sees it.
Carmichael's world has changed, but kettles, dishes and commutes are chores too. The hearth has moved, and the habit can move with it.

how: Some Christians today pray from Carmina Gadelica or from modern books of Celtic-style daily prayer, saying short blessings over chores, meals, journeys and sleep.

o: a single grace said once in the morning for all the day's meals
Gaelic prayers that bless daily chores like fire, milking and sleep
a priest's blessing that makes every object in a house holy

games.q: blessings for the day — tap the pairs.

s: the Gaelic blessings were only said in church
they were said at the hearth, in the cowshed, at the loom, on the road and at bedtime.
first Timothy says nothing is to be refused if it's received with thanksgiving
"every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving."
Carmina Gadelica is one poet's own verse
Alexander Carmichael collected blessings he heard from working people, though scholars note he edited and polished some of them.

games.q: it's morning in a Highland cottage and the fire has been banked all night. what happens in the old way?
o: the fire is lit in silence, and prayers wait for church.
the fire is kindled with a blessing, right there at the hearth.
the chore is skipped on holy days.
games.why: the holy moment isn't saved for later. lighting the fire is the moment.

practice: Pick a job you'll do later, the kettle, the dishes, the laundry, the drive, and see your hands doing it.

If you pray, borrow the words from Colossians, whatsoever ye do, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, and ask God's blessing on that job when it comes; if you don't, decide to do it slowly, with full attention, as if it mattered.

wordCard.voice: Blessings for everything. The Gaelic habit, written down in Carmina Gadelica, of blessing the fire, the milking, the road and sleep.

carryVoice: Your line: bless the fire. Lighting it can be the holy moment. See you tomorrow.
